paras: The killing of Pickens Pendergrass and threatened lynching of Summer Little took place near Heflin, Alabama, in May 1888, when Pendergrass, of Davisville, was shot dead and about forty armed citizens searched for Little, a Black man accused of the shooting, intending to lynch him. Alfred Newell, said to be implicated, was jailed at Edwardsville; Little remained at large.

According to a Davisville dispatch, Pendergrass, his brother-in-law John Smith and Will Holmes took a Saturday train to Heflin and walked home by a mountain trail. Lost a few miles out of Heflin, they stopped at the cabins of Summer Little to ask the way. The dispatch said the residents took the men for "suspicious characters" in a region where "illicit business" was believed to go on, and answered them with insults, to which Pendergrass, "slightly intoxicated," replied in "very plain language."

In this account, two Black men armed with a shotgun and a rifle followed the three unarmed men and overtook them about half a mile from the cabins. Alf Newell leveled the shotgun at Pendergrass and Holmes grabbed it, whereupon Little reached around Newell and fired the rifle, striking Pendergrass in the neck and killing him instantly between sundown and dark.

Newell was captured and "landed in Edwardsville jail," but Little escaped. About forty armed citizens then scoured the country, "bent on lynching the murderer," and the dispatch said there was "no doubt but Little will be mobbed if captured."
Pendergrass's body was brought home and buried at White Plains. No report of Little's capture, a lynching, or any trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached print through a single Davisville dispatch dated May 14. The Charlotte Messenger printed a condensed version on May 19 under the headline "Shooting in Davisville, Ala.," spelling the accused's name "Sumner." The Atlanta Constitution ran the full text on May 22 as "Another Alabama Tragedy," grouped with two unrelated Eufaula murders under "Blood in Alabama. A Couple of Senational Murders." Both called Little "the murderer", reported the lynching plan without comment, and gave only the Pendergrass party's side of the quarrel.

reader.title: Killing of Pickens Pendergrass and threatened lynching of Summer Little
bases: About forty armed citizens were reported searching the country for Summer Little, 'bent on lynching' him, after he was accused of shooting Pickens Pendergrass; no capture or lynching was reported (A1, A2).

A group of about forty armed citizens set out to lynch Little for the alleged killing of Pendergrass, but at last report he was still at large and no one had been killed by the crowd (A1, A2); the shooting of Pendergrass itself was by one or two men, not a mob.
Both articles print the same Davisville dispatch (A1 condensed, A2 in full), so they are one report rather than two independent accounts (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Davisville dispatch (Pendergrass party's version)
accounts.gist: Lost on a mountain trail, Pendergrass, Smith and Holmes asked at Little's cabins for directions, were insulted, and Pendergrass answered in 'very plain language'; two armed Black men followed the unarmed trio, Newell leveled a shotgun, Holmes grabbed it, and Little shot Pendergrass with a rifle.

accounts.label: Condensed wire report
accounts.gist: Pendergrass was shot and killed by Little near Heflin; Newell was jailed; forty armed citizens were searching to lynch Little, who would be 'mobbed if captured'.

framing.detail: The Atlanta Constitution ran the dispatch as 'Another Alabama Tragedy' under 'Blood in Alabama. A Couple of Senational Murders', calling Little 'the murderer' and reporting the lynching intent without comment.
The Charlotte Messenger printed a shortened version headed 'Shooting in Davisville, Ala.', keeping the forecast that Little 'will be mobbed if captured'.

conflicts.note: Spelling only; same dispatch. 'Sunmer' in A1's body is likely a typesetting or OCR slip for 'Sumner'.
